lesson_title: Aunt Lerato's Report Card: Analysis and Interpretation
hook_text: The books say the share is worth 500 cents. The cousins are paying 620. Who's wrong? Neither — and explaining why is the whole skill.
clip_script: Uncle Sipho's butchery has become a company, and he wants the family to buy in. Aunt Lerato, who has never trusted a smile in her life, asks for the books and rules up a report card. Can it pay this month's bills? More than two rand ready for every rand owed — and even if nobody buys another chop, still one rand twenty-five. How fast does the money turn? Customers settle in thirty days; the butchery pays its suppliers in fifty-two. The suppliers' patience is carrying the customers' slowness — clever, as long as the suppliers agreed to it. Would a terrible year sink it? It owns three times what it owes. Now the question the family really cares about: borrow at eleven, earn at eighteen. Every borrowed rand works FOR the family — that is gearing, and it is an amplifier: better good years, worse bad ones, always both. And the two numbers everyone confuses: the books say a share is worth 500 cents, but the cousins pay 620. They are not buying the mincer and the cold room — they are buying the future: next year's profits, the Saturday queue, Uncle Sipho's nose for good suppliers. None of that stands on a balance sheet. Compare, then judge. That reflex is the entire subject.
visual_style: A handwritten report card filling in mark by mark over butchery scenes; coins circling from cold room to counter to suppliers; a see-saw labelled eleven and eighteen tipping toward the family; two price tags on one share — 500 and 620 — with the gap glowing.
pacing: Steady question-answer rhythm through the report card, a lean-in beat on gearing, closing punch on the two price tags.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn the three-sentence answer that earns full interpretation marks.
